title: Sasanian silver-gilt ewer with dancing females within arcades — maenads of Dionysus, or the Iranian Anahita, and the Metropolitan Museum says it cannot tell
language_note:
Museum catalogue record in English. THE RECORD CARRIES NO SOURCE-LANGUAGE TEXT AND CLAIMS NONE. The object bears no inscription that the Met transcribes, and the only text here is the Museum's own object description, which on a find record is what `original_text_excerpt` holds.

FIRST RECORD IN THIS CORPUS WITH `source_type` `object_record`. The four FIND_TYPES are `find_record`, `coin_record`, `object_record` and `artefact_record`; the corpus used the first two, and `ingest/test_fidelity.py` exercises all four. A silver vessel with no findspot is not a find and is not a coin, and the vocabulary already held the right word.
date: ca. 6th–7th century CE, as the Metropolitan Museum dates it. Within the project's window (27 BC – 1204 AD) and contemporary with the late Sasanian court that the ŠKZ inscription's dynasty founded three centuries earlier.
findspot: NOT RECORDED, and absent rather than vague. The Met's credit line is `Purchase, Mr. and Mrs. C. Douglas Dillon Gift and Rogers Fund, 1967`; the record states a geography, `Iran`, and names no site, no excavation and no hoard. `persia-03-coin` is the corpus's precedent for saying so plainly instead of placing an object where nobody said it was.

origin_places.name: Iran — the geography the Metropolitan Museum records for this object, with no site named
origin_places.note: NO ID, AND NONE IS AVAILABLE HONESTLY. The Museum's `Geography` field reads `Iran` and its `Culture` field reads `Sasanian`; between them they name a modern state and a dynasty, and this corpus has refused a gazetteer id for `kēsar`, `Hrōmāy`, `mlk Rmn`, `mlk Frs¹` and `the King of the Axômites` on the rule that a people, a state, an office and a title are not settlements. A country is the same refusal one scale up. `regional` is what GROUNDS calls this exactly — only the region is known, the map is sparser, and that is correct.

original_text_excerpt: Late Sasanian silver vessels, particularly bottles and ewers, often were decorated with female figures holding a variety of festal objects. The appearance of these motifs attests to the continuing influence of Greek imagery associated with the wine god Dionysus. On this silver-gilt vessel, floral arches, supported by low pilasters, frame four dancing female figures. Each holds a ceremonial object in either hand: grape and leaf branches, a vessel, a heart-shaped flower. Beneath one arcade, birds peck at fruit, and beneath another a tiny panther drinks from a ewer. Both the females and their decorative motifs recall representations of the maenads, attendants of Dionysus. However, it has been suggested that these figures have been adapted to the cult of the Iranian goddess Anahita. No texts survive to explain the appearance or function of these female figures, but it seems likely that vessels decorated with motifs such as these would have been intended to hold wine for court celebrations or religious festivals.
original_text_note:
THE METROPOLITAN MUSEUM'S OWN OBJECT DESCRIPTION, VERBATIM AND ENTIRE, AND NOT ONE WORD OF THIS PROJECT'S PROSE IS IN IT. On a find record `classify_original` returns `('object_description', 'en', True)` for `source_type` in FIND_TYPES whatever the field contains, and `derive_record_tier` returns `catalogue_record` on the same test before it reads anything else. So this field is a museum's prose about an object and must never be read as the wording of a primary text. `africa-02-aksumite-coin` and `persia-03-coin` are the pattern.

VERIFIED BY DIGEST ACROSS TWO MACHINES, as records 44 to 47 were. Typed into a file on the bridge; the same span sliced independently out of the live page in the browser as `innerText` between `Late Sasanian silver vessels` and `View more`; SHA-256 computed on both machines and compared.

    chars 1023   sha256 e424b363437e2831ca5af334b17bbde5dcf086d60712b51303017904e02e044c

The span was also checked for what a reader cannot see: no newline, no non-breaking space, no double space anywhere in it. That check exists because the line-number gutter on `arabia-07-cih541` turned out to be forty-four U+00A0s, which a curator retyping the passage would have replaced with ordinary spaces and nobody would have noticed.

THE HEDGE THIS RECORD IS DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE FOR IS IN THIS FIELD, WHICH IS THE FIELD THE LOADER CHUNKS. It is not in `notes` and it is not in this note. F3 declared two gloss-capable records at record 26 and neither could ever pass, because both hedges were written into `original_text_note` — this one — which the loader does not chunk. The argument is in `notes`; the hedge itself is three sentences up, in the Museum's words.
citation: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, `Ewer with dancing females within arcades`, Sasanian, ca. 6th–7th century CE, object number 67.10a, b, Ancient West Asian Art. https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/325865 — read 2026-09-06.
citation_original:
THE SOURCE NAMES A LICENCE AND THE POSITION IS `open_licence_stated`. Quoted verbatim from https://www.metmuseum.org/about-the-met/policies-and-documents/open-access, read 2026-09-06:

"In February 2017, The Met introduced its Open Access Initiative, which makes images of public-domain artworks and basic data on all accessioned works in its collection available for unrestricted use under Creative Commons Zero (CC0)."

And from the object page itself, https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/325865, read the same day: the line `Public Domain` stands directly beneath the description.

THE CC0 GRANT IS CONDITIONAL AND THE CONDITION WAS CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. `data/met-licence-declaration.txt`, written for Block B4 on 2026-08-14, states the condition in terms: "The CC0 designation applies to PUBLIC-DOMAIN ARTWORKS ONLY. The Met's collection also contains objects that are not Open Access, and the API returns those too. CC0 is therefore a property of the individual object record, not of the API." The Met's own object-level flag was read for THIS object on 2026-09-06 — `collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/325865` returns `"isPublicDomain": true` — and it is recorded here rather than inferred from the collection.

WHY THE READING WAS REDONE AND NOT INHERITED. The existing declaration was written for a DIFFERENT USE. Its own scope section says Met object descriptions in this project "are used as DISTRACTORS ... They are never cited, never translated, never placed on the map, and never presented as evidence." This record cites one, places it and presents it as evidence. FINDING 69 was produced by two licence claims that were wrong in opposite directions in one session, and an inherited grant whose stated scope excludes the use it is being put to is the same error with a document in front of it.

WHY NOT `public_domain`: a licence IS named. `africa-07-cosmas-sasu` is `public_domain` precisely because no licence is named there — a dedication to the public domain is not a licence — and this page names CC0 in so many words. The object page's own `Public Domain` line is the artwork's copyright STATUS, which is the condition the CC0 grant rests on, and it is recorded above as that rather than as a second position.
notes:
F7's Persia `catalogue_record` slot — RULING 77's exchange half, the record Persia takes back after giving one up to Arabia in F6 so that `records_by_region_target_at_60` does not move. Persia ends Block F at 9 and Arabia at 8, exactly as ruling 44 declared.

THIS RECORD CARRIES F7's ONE `gloss_capable` DECLARATION, THE LAST IN BLOCK F, AND THE KIND IS `hedged_identification`. Everything the declaration needs is inside `original_text_excerpt`, which the loader chunks and the model sees:

(a) A GENUINE ALTERNATIVE READING, and it is the Museum's, not this project's — "Both the females and their decorative motifs recall representations of the maenads, attendants of Dionysus. However, it has been suggested that these figures have been adapted to the cult of the Iranian goddess Anahita."

(b) A STATEMENT THAT THE READING IS UNCERTAIN, twice over and in the same paragraph — "it has been suggested", and then the flat admission "No texts survive to explain the appearance or function of these female figures".

FINDING 55 is the rule this satisfies: an alternative this project supplied itself is worth nothing. Not one word of the hedge is ours. `arabia-07-cih541` is the pattern and it is F6's, where the uncertain-reading mark, the variant and the definition of both were all quoted from DASI.

SECOND `hedged_identification` IN THE CORPUS, after `eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun`. The declared list closes at 7 of 7: five `contested_reading` and two `hedged_identification`. AND ONE DECLARATION ONLY — a second is over-delivery that `check_delivery` fails on the day it happens, so the other six F7 records carry none however declarable their material looks.

WHY THE DISPUTE IS THE PROJECT'S OWN QUESTION. Every other gloss case in this corpus is about what a text SAYS — which characters are on a stone, which of two editors read a sign correctly. This one is about what an image MEANS, and the two readings are the two halves of Mundus Ulterior: either a Sasanian court silversmith was drawing Greek maenads, or an Iranian goddess had taken over the Greek figures' clothes. A museum says, in its own catalogue, that it cannot tell which. That is the world beyond Rome reading Rome's images and leaving the reading open, and it is argued by the institution about the object rather than by this project about a text.

WHAT PERSIA DID NOT HAVE, AND WHAT THIS ADDS. The corpus's Persia records are two royal inscriptions (ŠKZ, Abnun), a Middle Persian geography, a British Museum drachm, a British Museum silver plate, and `persia-04-bronze-heracles` — a Greek Heracles identified with the Iranian Verethragna. That last one asks exactly this record's question about a cult bronze; this one asks it about court silver, four centuries later and at the other end of the empire's life. RULING 79's P3 is denominated on precisely that resemblance and predicts this record crowds `bronze-heracles-verethragna-from-mesene` and nothing else in the run.

THE DISTRACTOR CHECK, WHICH HAD TO BE MADE AND HAD NEVER BEEN MADE BEFORE. This corpus's distractor set is drawn from the Metropolitan Museum — 393 chunks of it, ingested in Block B4 — so a Met object entering the SEED corpus is the first opportunity this project has had to put the same object in the index twice under two roles, once as evidence and once as known-irrelevant padding. `data/distractors/met-2026-08-14.json` was searched on 2026-09-06 for both `325865` and `67.10a` and contains neither. Block B3's rule would have kept it out anyway — distractors are restricted to material with no Roman-contact dimension, and Sasanian silver with Dionysiac imagery is the opposite of that — but a rule that would have prevented a collision is not the same thing as checking that it did.

NOT THE BEST ROME–PERSIA OBJECT AVAILABLE, AND THE BETTER ONE WAS REFUSED FOR AN INSTRUMENT REASON. The BnF's sardonyx cameo of Shapur I seizing the emperor Valerian by the wrist (`camée.360`, ARK `c33gbqh22`) opens, has a permalink, and carries the BnF's own argument that a Roman hand carved it. Its description is in French, and by FINDING 86 a French object description on a find record enters this index declared English, exactly as a Thai one does. `F7_CURATION_START.md` records it as a searched failure under ruling 75.
